passages.original: — 11. AUributa per Hilarium singulis personis. Trinitas in rebus factis repræsentatur. Quidam cum vellet brevissirne singularum in Trinitate personarum insinuare propria, Æternitas, inquit, in Patre, species in Imagine, usus in Munere. Et quia non mediocris auctoritalis in tractatione Scripturarum, et assertione fidei vir exstitit ; Hilarius enin hoc in libris suis posuit (Lib. 2 de TrinUale)\ horum verborum, id est, Patris, et Imaginis, et Muneris, aeternitatis, et speciei, et usus, abditam scrutatus intelligentiam quantum valeo, non eum secutum arbitror in æternitatis vocabulo, nisi quod Pater non habet Patrem de quo sit, Filins autem de Patre est ut sit, atqne ut illi coæternus sit.
passages.english: — 11. The attributes assigned by Hilary to the individual persons. The Trinity is represented in created things. A certain writer, wishing to suggest as briefly as possible what is proper to each of the persons in the Trinity, said: "Eternity in the Father, form in the Image, use in the Gift." And since he was a man of no small authority in the treatment of the Scriptures and in the defence of the faith (for it was Hilary who set this down in his books), I have searched out, as far as I am able, the hidden meaning of these words, that is, of "Father", "Image" and "Gift", of "eternity", "form" and "use". I do not think he followed any other sense in the word "eternity" than this: that the Father has no father from whom he is, whereas the Son is from the Father, so that he is, and so that he is coeternal with him.
passages.notes: The opening "— 11." and the heading are editorial chapter/section matter. The bracketed reference "(Lib. 2 de Trinitate)" in the edition, i.e. Hilary, On the Trinity book 2, has been omitted from the translation as an editorial citation. "Species" is rendered "form"; it can also mean "beauty", as the following context shows.

passages.original: CAPUT V. - 8. De eadem re. An forte illud est quod nos ab his angustiis possit eruere, ut quoniam diximus ibi quosque posuisse beatam vitam quod eos maxime delectavit, ut voluptas Epicurum , virtus Zenonem ; sic alium aliquid aliud, nihil dicamus esse beate vivere, nisi vivere sccundum delectationem suam , et ideo falsum non esse quod omnes beate vivere velint, quia omnes iIa volunt ut quemque delectat ?
passages.english: CHAPTER V. - 8. On the same subject. Or perhaps this is what can rescue us from these difficulties: since we said that each person placed the happy life in what most delighted him, as pleasure [did for] Epicurus and virtue [for] Zeno, and so another [placed it in] something else, should we say that living happily is nothing other than living according to one's own delight, and that it is therefore not false that all wish to live happily, because all wish [to live] as it delights each one?

passages.original: Ideo igitur id vult quod potest , quoniam quod vult non potest. Hæc est tota , utrum ridenda, an potius miseranda , superborum beatitudo mortalium , gloriantium se vivere ut volunt, quia volentes patienter ferunt quæ accidere sibi nolunt. Hoc est enim , aiunt, quod sapienter dixit Terentius , Quoniam non potest a.id Ueri quod vis, Id velis qUod Andreia, i, 5, 6. possis 9, (In act. scen, vers. ) Commode hoc dictum esse, quis negat? Sed consilium est datum misero, ne esset miserior.
passages.english: Therefore he wills what he can, since he cannot [have] what he wills. This is the whole happiness of proud mortals (whether to be laughed at or rather pitied), who boast that they live as they will, because they bear willingly and patiently the things they do not will to happen to them. For this, they say, is what Terence said wisely: "Since what you want cannot happen, want what you can." Who denies that this was aptly said? But it was advice given to a wretched man, so that he might not be more wretched.
passages.notes: The quotation is from Terence, Andria (Act 2, scene 1, lines 5–6); the edition's references embedded in the quotation have been omitted.

passages.original: Sed quodlibet horum esset, cliam in boc libro apparuit Trinitatis æqualitas, et non Dens triplex, sed Trinitas : nec quasi aliquid duplum esse Patrem et Filium ad simplum Spiritum sanctum ; ubi nee tria plus aliquid sunt quam unum horum. Disputatum est eliam quomodo possit intelligi quod ait Hilarius ppiscopus': Æternitas in Patre, species in Imagine, usu: in Munere. In septimo, quæstio quæ dilata fuerat, explicatur, ita ut Dens qui genuit Filium, non solum sit Pater virtutis ct sapientiæ suæ, sed etiam ipse virtus atque sapientia;
passages.english: But whichever of these it might be, in this book too the equality of the Trinity became evident, and that God is not threefold but a Trinity; nor are the Father and the Son as it were something double in relation to the single Holy Spirit, since there three are not anything more than one of them. It was also discussed how what Bishop Hilary says can be understood: "Eternity in the Father, form in the Image, use in the Gift." In the seventh [book], the question which had been postponed is explained, so that God who begot the Son is not only the Father of his own power and wisdom, but is also himself power and wisdom;
passages.notes: This is from Augustine's summary of the earlier books (Book 15); "this book" refers to Book 6.
